title: How integers are stored, and where they break
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain two's complement, predict what happens at the limits of a type, and recognise the integer bugs that turn into security findings.

blocks.text: An integer is a fixed number of bits. Everything surprising about integer arithmetic in C follows from that one fact: there is no room for a value outside the range, so something has to happen at the edges — and what happens differs between signed and unsigned in a way that matters.
Two's complement: how negative numbers are stored

blocks.caption: Four bits, sixteen values
lines: 1000       8        -8     <- the sign bit flips the meaning
1111      15        -1     <- all ones is -1, not the largest
/* To negate: flip every bit, then add one. */

blocks.title: Why this representation won
blocks.text: With two's complement the hardware adds signed and unsigned values with the same circuit — subtraction is just addition of the negation, and there is only one zero. The cost is an asymmetric range: with 32 bits you get -2147483648 to 2147483647, so the most negative value has no positive counterpart. That asymmetry is a real source of bugs.
The limits, and what lives at them

blocks.caption: Print them rather than memorising them
lines: printf("%d\n", -n);             /* undefined — the positive value does not exist */
printf("%d\n", abs(INT_MIN));   /* undefined for the same reason */

blocks.caption: One is defined, one is not
lines: u = u + 1;              /* 0 — defined: unsigned wraps modulo 2^N */
s = s + 1;              /* undefined behaviour — anything may happen */
/* Checking BEFORE the operation is the only correct approach: */
int sum = a + b;        /* now safe */
/* Or use the compiler builtins where available: */

blocks.title: Three integer bugs that become security findings
blocks.text: First: a size computed as count * item_size wraps to something small, so the allocation is too small and the following writes overflow the buffer. Second: a length read as a signed value arrives negative, converts to a huge size_t, and passes every bounds check. Third: subtracting two lengths produces a negative that becomes enormous when used as a size. All three are arithmetic that looks ordinary and produces a memory-safety failure.
Writing arithmetic that cannot surprise you

items: Use size_t for sizes, counts, and indices — and validate before converting anything into it
Check for overflow before the operation, never by inspecting the result afterwards
Prefer calloc(n, size) over malloc(n * size) so the multiplication is checked for you
Compare a - b > limit as a > limit + b where possible, so no subtraction can go negative
Use the fixed-width types from <stdint.h> when the range must be the same everywhere
Turn on -fsanitize=undefined in development so signed overflow is reported rather than assumed away

blocks.caption: Narrowing and sign changes
lines: char  c   = big;          /* keeps the low 8 bits: 44 */
unsigned int u = neg;     /* becomes UINT_MAX — the bits are unchanged, the reading is not */
int   narrow = wide;      /* value does not fit: implementation-defined */
/* -Wconversion warns about these; it is worth enabling on new code. */

blocks.title: Walk off the edge on purpose
steps: Print INT_MAX, INT_MIN, UINT_MAX and SIZE_MAX from <limits.h> and <stdint.h>
Run: int s = INT_MAX; s = s + 1; printf("%d\n", s);   at -O0 and again at -O2
Run the same with -fsanitize=undefined and read the report
Run: unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u = u + 1; printf("%u\n", u);   and note it is defined
Print (unsigned)(-1) and explain the result from the bit pattern
Write a size check with a signed length of -1 and watch it pass the bounds test
Rewrite it to reject negatives at the boundary and confirm it now fails correctly
blocks.expected: Signed overflow behaving differently at two optimisation levels and being named by the sanitizer, defined unsigned wrapping, and a bounds check that passes a negative length until you fix it. That last one is the shape behind a long list of real advisories.

cheatsheet: Integers are a fixed number of bits; everything surprising follows from that
Two's complement: negate by flipping all bits and adding one; all ones is -1
The range is asymmetric: -INT_MIN and abs(INT_MIN) are undefined
Unsigned overflow wraps and is defined; signed overflow is undefined
Check for overflow BEFORE the operation, or use __builtin_*_overflow
Use size_t for sizes and validate before converting into it
A negative length converted to size_t becomes enormous and passes bounds checks
calloc(n, size) checks the multiplication that malloc(n * size) does not
<stdint.h> fixed-width types when the range must be identical everywhere

checkpoint.prompt: In two's complement, what value does a byte of all ones represent when read as signed?
checkpoint.explanation: All ones is -1. The same bits read as unsigned are 255 — the bit pattern does not change, only the interpretation.

choices.A: Negation is not defined for signed types
choices.B: It is defined and equals INT_MAX
choices.C: The range is asymmetric — the positive counterpart of INT_MIN does not exist in the type

checkpoint.explanation: With 32 bits the range is -2147483648 to 2147483647. There is one more negative value than positive, and abs(INT_MIN) has the same problem.

checkpoint.prompt: How should you check that a + b will not overflow?

choices.A: Test before adding, for example if (a > 0 && b > INT_MAX - a), or use __builtin_add_overflow
choices.C: Compute the sum and test whether it is smaller than a
choices.D: Use an assert after the addition

checkpoint.explanation: Testing the result relies on the overflow having happened, which is undefined — so the compiler may remove the check entirely.

checkpoint.prompt: A length arrives as a signed -1 and is used as a size_t. What is the security consequence?

choices.C: It becomes an enormous positive value that passes every bounds check and is then used as a size

checkpoint.explanation: This is one of the most repeated patterns in real advisories. Reject negative lengths at the boundary, before any conversion happens.
